神樂鈴主要由黃銅或青銅鑄製的球形金屬外殼構成，外殼表面多採用金色或銀色打磨工藝。: The kagura suzu is mainly a spherical metal shell cast in brass or bronze, its surface usually worked to a gold or silver finish. Inside are several small metal balls, usually of iron or likewise of brass. A slight gap between the balls and the shell lets them strike freely when the bell is shaken. The handle is often wood, such as hinoki or cypress, for the player to grip. On some finer instruments the metal parts carry finely engraved decoration.
神樂鈴為手持短柄的體鳴樂器，鈴分三層懸掛於中央柄上。傳統神樂舞中由巫女持握短柄，: The kagura suzu is a hand-held idiophone on a short handle, its bells hung in three tiers from the central shaft. In the traditional kagura dance a miko holds the short handle and shakes it to sound the bells. The source gives no teaching detail, so only the basic order is given here: grip the short handle and let the bells hang down, then shake the handle so that the bells sound.
神樂鈴用於神樂舞蹈。神樂一詞最早於773年見於宮廷曲目，源自鄉村民間傳統，後成為: The kagura suzu is used in kagura dance. The word kagura first appears in 773, in a court programme; it came from rural folk tradition, later became an important part of the Japanese imperial tradition and is regarded as one of the nation's important artistic traditions. In myth, Amenouzume dances holding a sakaki branch, which is taken as the ancient prototype of the kagura suzu. Small bell trees are held and performed by miko, while large bells hang before shrines and are sounded with a robe or silk ribbon, showing the instrument's long association with Shinto ritual and folk festivals.
神樂鈴音色清脆明亮，具有高度穿透力，常帶有閃爍的金屬光澤感。其音域集中在高頻區域: The kagura suzu has a clear, bright timbre with strong carrying power, often with a glittering metallic sheen. Its range sits in the high frequencies, the tone pure and lively, well able to suggest something light and sacred. The design — a spherical metal shell with small balls inside — produces idiophonic resonance when shaken or struck; the sound is crisp and short, with no long sustain. Against the triangle of Western music the kagura suzu sounds softer and more intimate, with an Eastern religious atmosphere; against a Chinese temple bell it is clearer and brighter. Its characteristic layering of sounds creates a rippling wash, and it is often used in religious ritual to set a solemn mood.
神樂鈴（Kagura Suzu）是日本神道儀式中的體鳴樂器，由十二至十五枚小鈴分: The kagura suzu is an idiophone of Japanese Shinto ritual, made of twelve to fifteen small bells hung in three tiers from a short handle: two on the top tier, four in the middle and six at the bottom, suspended on coiled brass wire. The player holds the short handle and shakes it to sound the bells, as is common in kagura dance; it also appears in folk and ritual settings. Large bells may hang before a shrine and be set sounding with a robe or sash, while small ones are mostly held by miko.
